text: The last three lessons covered why documentation matters, how a diagram and a runbook work together, and how to write for a reader who doesn't share your context. This lesson closes out the chapter by turning all of that into one concrete checklist you can actually run through, item by item, before telling someone 'it's yours now.'

First three items. Is the architecture diagram current -- not the version from day one, but today's actual layout? An outdated diagram is often worse than none at all, because it's trusted by default. Is the runbook written, with the specific tasks, contacts, and log locations from Lesson 22, not a vague summary? And is access actually transferred -- not just described on paper, but granted, so the new owner can log in and act, not just read about it?

Second three items. Are monitoring and alerting contacts updated, so a real alert pages someone who can still act on it, instead of someone who's already gone? Is the backup and disaster recovery procedure documented as an actual restore process, not just a note that backups exist, so nobody improvises during a real emergency? And are known issues and technical debt named explicitly, so the new owner inherits them on purpose instead of discovering them mid-incident?

Put together, that's six boxes: diagram current, runbook written, access transferred, alert contacts updated, backup and DR documented, known issues noted. Each one exists because skipping it has caused a real, specific problem on real teams -- this isn't a theoretical list, and none of the six items is optional just because the environment happens to be running fine today.

Treat this checklist the way you'd treat a pre-flight checklist, not a form signed quickly on the way out the door. Any unchecked item means the handoff isn't actually done yet, the same bar this chapter opened with for a deployment itself. Next, chapter seven: the five places a new deployment usually breaks.
